narrative:
The model estimated a 54.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a slightly-more-likely-than-not prediction, not a certainty, but because admission was tied to predicted bar success, it was enough to lead to rejection.

The strongest reason was your third-year class-rank position. You were in the lowest decile (1) at your school, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile (5.79). This was the most influential factor and it pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score of 36 was the second most important factor. Although it is slightly below the accepted-student average of 37.18, its overall role in your prediction was favorable: it pushed toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.00, compared with an accepted-student average of 3.23, was the third most important factor and also worked in your favor, pushing toward passing. In other words, the model saw real strengths in your LSAT and GPA, but your very low third-year rank outweighed them.

To improve your chances, speak with the admissions office or a pre-law advisor about why the rank was low and whether you can address it. Consider retaking the LSAT if you can reasonably improve, strengthening your academic record if further coursework is possible, and reapplying after adding evidence of readiness for law study. Provide context for any unusual grading or personal circumstances, and ask whether a waitlist, conditional admission, or delay is possible.
